title.en: The King of the Great World Invades Ireland
title.zh: 大世界之王入侵愛爾蘭

region.en: Fionntulach (the White Hill), Co. Kerry, Ireland

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book II, ch. I, eBook #14465

summary.en: The greatest battle the Fianna ever fought begins: Daire Donn, High King of the Great World, gathers the kings of Greece, France, Lochlann, the Dog-Heads and Cat-Heads, and Ogarmach the best woman-warrior of the world, to put Ireland under tribute. The exiled traitor Glas son of Bremen pilots them to Ireland, and only a shore of white sand at Corca Duibhne will do for the fairs and gatherings of so vast an army.
summary.zh: 菲亞納最宏偉之戰拉開序幕：大世界至高王達爾·東召集希臘、法蘭西、洛赫蘭諸王，犬首族、貓首族，以及世上最強女戰士奧加馬克，欲使愛爾蘭納貢。被逐出的叛徒格拉斯引艦隊入愛爾蘭，唯有科爾卡·迪夫尼的白沙灘足以容納此大軍的集市與集會。

sensitivity.note: The White Strand (Finntraigh) war-cycle is a world-invasion apocalypse of the Fenian cycle; the Dog-Headed and Cat-Headed peoples are marvel-races standard in voyage literature. Pin symbolic at the Kerry coast.

passages.text: Of all the great battles the Fianna fought to keep the foreigners out of Ireland, the greatest was the one that was fought at Finntraigh the White Strand, in Munster. One time the enemies of Ireland gathered together under Daire Donn, High King of the Great World, thinking to take Ireland and to put it under tribute. The King of Greece was of them, and the King of France, and the King of the Eastern World, and Lughman of the Broad Arms, King of the Saxons, and Tor the son of Breogan, King of the Great Plain, and Comur of the Crooked Sword, King of the Men of the Dog-Heads, and Caitchenn, King of the Men of the Cat-Heads, and Caisel of the Feathers, King of Lochlann, and three kings from the rising of the sun in the east, and Ogarmach, daughter of the King of Greece, the best woman-warrior that ever came into the world, and a great many other kings and great lords.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: The King of the World asked then: "Who is there can give me knowledge of the harbours of Ireland?" "I will do that for you, and I will bring you to a good harbour," said Glas, son of Bremen, that had been put out of Ireland by Finn for doing some treachery. Then the armies set out in their ships, and they were not gone far when the wind rose and the waves, and they could hear nothing but the wild playing of the sea-women, and the screams of frightened birds, and the breaking of ropes and of sails.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: But after a while, when the wind found no weakness in the heroes, it rose from them and went up into its own high place, and the sea grew quiet and the harbours friendly. They stopped for a while at an island that was called the Green Rock; but the King of the World said: "It is not a harbour like this you promised me, Glas, but a shore of white sand where my armies could have their fairs and their gatherings the time they would not be fighting." "I know a harbour of that sort in the west of Ireland," said Glas, "the Harbour of the White Strand in Corca Duibhne." So they went into their ships again, and went on over the sea towards Ireland.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. I; not verbatim.

title.zh: 克爾的求婚詩贏得克蕾德

region.en: Loch Cuire, Paps of Dana, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡達娜山嶽庫雷湖

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book II, ch. II, eBook #14465

summary.en: Gathering the Fianna against the invaders, Finn's host feeds on the nuts of the hazels of Cenntire and the salmon of Luimnech. Cael, who saw in a dream a woman of the Sidhe, wins Credhe daughter of the King of Ciarraighe Luachra by a poem no man can match — an inventory of her bowls, horns, crystal vats, apple-tree over the vat of bronze, and her house thatched with the crimson wings of birds — and she joins the march to the White Strand with a herd of cattle for the war.
summary.zh: 菲亞納出征集結，取食辛提里榛樹之果與利默里克之鮭。克爾曾夢見仙姬，今以無人能及之詩贏得西拉格·盧赫拉王之女克蕾德——詩中細數她的酒碗、牛角杯、水晶缸、銅缸上的蘋果樹，以及以緋紅鳥翼為瓦的宮室。她攜牛群隨軍出征白沙灘。

sensitivity.note: The courtship-poem (love-service verse) is the Fenian wedding-custom motif; Credhe is a Sidhe-bride from the Paps of Dana — the mountain named for the goddess Danu. The dream-woman motif links to the bruiden genre.

passages.text: When it was shown to Finn that the enemies of Ireland were coming, he called together the seven battalions of the Fianna, and the place where they gathered was on the hill that was called Fionntulach, the White Hill, in Munster. They had every sort of thing for food there, beautiful blackberries, haws of the hawthorn, nuts of the hazels of Cenntire, watercress at the beginning of summer; and birds out of the oak-woods, speckled eggs from the cliffs, and salmon out of Luimnech, and eels of the Sionnan. As they were going to set out southwards they saw one of their young men, Gael, grandson of Nemhnain, coming towards them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: "It was about a high marriage and a woman of the Sidhe that was showed to me in a dream I was speaking with my nurse at Brugh na Boinne; Credhe it was I saw, daughter of the King of Ciarraighe Luachra." "Do you know this, Cael, that she is the greatest deceiver of all the women of Ireland? She will let no one come unless he is able to make a poem setting out the report of her bowls and her horns and her cups, her grand vessels and all her palaces." "I have all that ready," said Cael.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: They came to the door of the hill of the Sidhe at Loch Cuire and knocked at it with the shafts of their long gold-socketted spears, and Credhe herself came out, having three times fifty women with her. Cael rose up and sang his poem: "A journey I have to make, and it is no easy journey, to the house of Credhe against the breast of the mountain, at the Paps of Dana... There is a vat there of royal bronze, the juice of pleasant malt is running from it; over the vat is an apple-tree with its heavy fruit; when Credhe's horn is filled from the vat, four apples fall into it together...
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: She that owns all these things both at low water and at flood, Credhe from the Hill of the Three Peaks, she is beyond all the women of Ireland by the length of a spear-cast." Then Credhe took him for her husband, and the wedding-feast was made, and the whole of the Fianna stopped there through seven days at drinking and pleasure. And through the whole length of the battle that followed, that lasted a year and a day, she had new milk for them, and it was to her house the wounded were brought for healing.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. II; not verbatim.

title.en: Conn Crither and the Sisters of the Country of the Young
title.zh: 康恩·克里瑟與青春之國三姐妹

region.en: Finntraigh (White Strand), Corca Duibhne, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡科爾卡·迪夫尼白沙灘

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book II, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: The watchman Conn Crither sleeps through the landing of the invaders and wakes to flames and cries. Swearing to sell his life dearly, he is met on the way by three sisters from Tir nan Og who have all given him their love: they raise Druid armies from stalks of grass and watercress, blind the enemy with a mist, and keep a well of healing at the foot of the Eagle's Mountain. Alone he routs a province's worth of the foe and takes the head of the King of the Great Plain, boasting he will not leave it until the Fianna come.
summary.zh: 哨兵康恩·克里瑟在敵軍登陸時睡著，醒來見火光哭聲四起。他誓要戰死沙場，途中遇見三位來自青春之國的仙姝——她們皆已屬意於他：她們以草莖與水芹編成德魯伊幻軍，以霧障敵眼，並在鷹山麓保有療傷之泉。他獨自擊潰一省之敵，斬大平原王之首，誇言非至菲亞納來援不棄其首。

sensitivity.note: The healing well (Slieve Iolair) is the Fenian analogue of the Greek Kallichoron-style wound-restoring springs — tagged 'resurrection' for its wound-to-wholeness function, not a religious claim. The three sisters are the triple fairy-mistress pattern.

passages.text: The man that was keeping watch at the White Strand was Conn Crither, son of Bran, from Teamhair Luachra, and after he had been a long time watching, he fell asleep one night west from the Round Hill of the Fianna, called Cruachan Adrann; and while he was in his sleep the ships came, and what roused him was the noise of the breaking of shields and the clashing of swords, and the cries of women and children and of dogs and horses that were under flames. Conn Crither started up and said: "It is great trouble has come on the people through my sleep; and I will not stay living after this for Finn and the Fianna of Ireland to see me, but I will rush into the middle of the strangers, and they will fall by me till I fall by them."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the way he saw three women dressed in battle clothes, and fast as he ran he could not overtake them. "Hold your hand," the nearest said, "for we are not come to harm you but to help you. We are three sisters, and we are come from Tir nan Og, the Country of the Young, and we have all three given you our love. We will make Druid armies about you from stalks of grass and from the tops of the watercress, and they will cry out to the strangers and will strike their arms from their hands, and take from them their strength and their eyesight.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: And we will put a Druid mist about you that will hide you from the armies of the strangers. And we have a well of healing at the foot of Slieve Iolair, the Eagle's Mountain, and its waters will cure every wound made in battle; and after bathing in that well you will be as whole and as sound as the day you were born." Conn Crither hurried on to the strand, took their spoils from the armies of the King of the Great Plain with the Druid army about him, fought the King himself, struck off his head, and lifted it up: "I will not let myself be parted from this body till some of the Fianna, few or many, will come to me."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: Glas son of Bremen Returns to Ireland
title.zh: 布雷門之子格拉斯歸國

region.en: Finntraigh (White Strand), Corca Duibhne, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡科爾卡·迪夫尼白沙灘

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book II, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Sent by the King of the World to identify the lone warrior boasting on the strand, Glas son of Bremen finds his own kinsman Conn Crither and turns his coat: no treasure of the world would keep him fighting against his blood once Finn's protection is promised. He asks the King to send his men one at a time, slaughters Madan of the Bent Neck in single combat, and his daily reports become the road by which the invaders are bled.
summary.zh: 大世界之王遣格拉斯去查明海灘上獨自誇耀的戰士是誰，格拉斯發現竟是自己族人康恩·克里瑟，隨即倒戈：只要芬恩許以庇護，世上任何財寶都不能令他與血親為敵。他請求國王逐一遣人上陣，單挑擊殺「彎頸」馬丹，其每日戰報遂成敵軍失血之路。

sensitivity.note: Traitor-redeemed is a Fenian stock figure; the single-combat tolling of the invaders runs through the whole cycle (compare Cuchulain's guard at the ford of the Tain). Prophesy aside: 'it was not in the prophecy that Glas would find his death there' shows the fate-motif of the Irish hero-tale.

passages.text: The King of the World heard the boast of the man on the strand and said: "Rise up now, Glas, son of Dremen, and see which of the Fianna of Ireland it is that is saying it." Glas left the ship and went to where Conn Crither was, and asked who was he. "I am Conn Crither, son of Bran, from Teamhair Luachra." "If that is so," said Glas, "you are of the one blood with myself, for I am Glas, son of Bremen from Teamhair Luachra." "It is not right for you to come fighting against me from those foreigners," said Conn. "It is a pity indeed; and but for Finn and the Fianna driving me from them, I would not fight against you or one of themselves for all the treasures of the whole world." "Do not say that, for I swear by my hand of valour, if you had killed Finn's own son and the sons of his people along with him, you need not be in dread of him if only you came under his word and his protection."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: "I think indeed the day is come for me to fight beside you," said Glas, and he went back to the King of the World and asked him not to let his armies land till the Fianna came, but to let one man only come to fight with each of them until that time. So two of the strangers were sent against them that day, and they got their death by Glas and by Conn Crither; then two men against each of them, and three times nine fell by them before night. And Conn Crither, covered with wounds, was bathed in the well of healing by the three sisters and made whole.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: And Glas went down to the harbour: "O King of the World, there is a friend of mine in the ships, Madan of the Bent Neck, son of the King of the Marshes; and it is what he said in the great world in the east, that he himself would be enough to take Ireland for you. I ask you to let him come alone against me to-night, till we see which of us will fight best for Ireland." So Madan came to the land, and the two made a very hard fight; but as it was not in the prophecy that Glas would find his death there, it was the son of the King of the Marshes that got his death by him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. IV; not verbatim.

title.en: The Men of Dea Come to the White Strand

region.en: Dun Sesnain, Ui Conall Gabra, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡塞斯南堡

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book II, ch. V, eBook #14465

summary.en: When Taistellach carries the alarm, Bran son of Febal goes to the Tuatha de Danaan feasting at Dun Sesnain. Dolb shames Bodb Dearg with the reminder that every king's son and Fianna leader has a wife or mother of the Sidhe, and the god-host musters in silk shirts and green shields — Midhir, Lir, Ilbrec son of Manannan, Abarthach, the Silver Hand, the Man of Sweet Speech. Abarthach slays the King of the Cat-Heads and, leaping down between Lir and the Dog-Head king, cuts off his legs at the knees and takes his head.
summary.zh: 泰斯特拉赫報警後，費巴爾之子布蘭前往在塞斯南堡設宴的神族。多爾布提醒波德·迪爾格：每位王子與菲亞納首領皆有一位仙族之妻母——神族遂著絲衫持綠盾集結：米德、利爾、瑪那南之子伊爾布雷克、阿巴爾塔赫、銀手、甜語者。阿巴爾塔赫斬貓首族王，又躍入利爾與犬首族王之間，斷其雙膝，取其首級。

sensitivity.note: The mythic-religious feature here is the alliance of the Tuatha de Danaan with their mortal kin — the aftermath of the Milesian settlement in reverse; the marvel-kings (Dog-Heads, Cat-Heads) belong to the Fenian marvel-race repertoire. Pin symbolic at Dun Sesnain.

passages.text: Taistellach that was one of Finn's messengers came to the White Strand asking news, and Conn bade him go back to where Finn was and tell him the way things were; and he sent him on to-night to the house of Bran, son of Febal his father, at Teamhair Luachra, to bid him gather all the Tuatha de Danaan to help them. Bran went out to gather the Tuatha de Danaan, and he went to Dun Sesnain in Ui Conall Gabra, where they were holding a feast at that time, and there he found Ilbrec the Many Coloured, son of Manannan, and Nemanach the Pearly, son of Angus Og, and Sigmall, grandson of Midhir.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: "There is a greater thing than this for you to do, Men of Dea," said Bran, and he told them the whole story. Dolb, son of Sesnan, went to Sidhe Bean Finn above Magh Femen to Bodb Dearg: "Young man," said Bodb Dearg, "we are no way bound to help the men of Ireland out of that strait." "Do not say that, for there is not a king's son or a prince or a leader of the Fianna of Ireland without having a wife or a mother or a foster-mother or a sweetheart of the Tuatha de Danaan; and it is good help they have given you every time you were in want of it."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: "I give my word," said Bodb Dearg, "it is right to give a good answer to so good a messenger." He sent word to the Tuatha de Danaan in every place, and they gathered to him, and their leaders besides Bodb Dearg were Midhir of Bri Leith, and Lir of Sidhe Finnachaidh, and Ilbrec, son of Manannan, and Argat Lamh, the Silver Hand, from the Sionnan, and the Man of Sweet Speech from the Boinn. "O Men of Dea," said Abarthach, "let a high mind and high courage rise within you now in the face of the battle, for the doings of every one among you will be told till the end of the world." The King of the Dog-Heads and the King of the Cat-Heads went against them with five red-armed battalions like great red waves.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: Lir attacked the King of the Dog-Heads and was getting the worst of it, and Ilbrec and Sigmall and the five sons of Finnaistucan were all driven off; but Abarthach made an end of the King of the Cat-Heads, rose on his spear, made a leap, and came down between Lir and his enemy. He took his sword in his left hand, made a thrust with his spear through the king's armour, and as the king raised up his shield he cut off both his legs at the knees, and the king let fall his shield, and Abarthach struck off his head.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book II, ch. V; not verbatim.
